Twenty-three comments

One of the best-known and best-loved of all ancient tunes, but I’m not sure whether there is a specific celtic origin, let alone Irish. One theory is that the tune was composed by King Henry VIII of England, who, amongst his other accomplishments, was apparently considered to be not a bad musician.
Trevor

↳ Posted by fidicen on April 17th, 2003.

Yeah, and was anyone going to tell him he wasn’t?

↳ Posted by Zina Lee on April 17th, 2003.

I’ve yet to come across this one in a session, but I have heard it said that it is of Irish origin. As Trevor says, it is sometimes attributed to Henry VIII (not an Irishman), but it is more likely that he was only responsible for the words to ‘Greensleeves’ (one of many poems that have been set to this air). I believe this or similar melodies appear in manuscripts, either as song airs or dance tunes, dating from before the reign of Henry VIII, some of them claiming it to be Irish.

The Oxford Book of Carols has a text for New Year which is a slightly adapted version to their source (“New Christmas Carols, 1642 … in the unique black-letter collection of Anthony à Wood”). Apparently, there should be three more verses…

1. The old year now away is fled,
The new year it is entered,
Then led us now our sins down-tread,
And joyfully all appear:

Let’s merry be this day,
And let us now both sport and play:
Hang grief, cast care away!
God send you a happy new year!

2. The name-day now of Christ we keep,
Who for our sins did often weep;
His hands and feet were wounded deep,
And his blessed side with a spear;

His head they crowned with thorn,
And at him they did laugh and scorn,
Who for our good was born:
God send us a happy New Year!

3.And now with New Year’s gifts each friend
Unto each other they do send:
God grant we may all our lives amend,
And that the truth may appear.

Now, like the snake, your skin cast off,
of evil thoughts and sin,
And so the year begin:
God send us a happy New Year!

Re: Greensleeves

I’m going to play some winter/holiday tunes at an informal recital. I took 5 of Falkbeer’s variations and tweaked them a little, and stuck it in the middle of a tweaked Dargason (half following an ABC I downloaded here and half by transposing chunks of the score to Holst’s 2nd Suite for Military Band) and made a little Holst/Vaughan Williams set I’m calling “English Christmas Dances with Gustav and Ralph”. In the “composer” section of my music editing app, I said “Traditionals arranged based on Holst and Vaughan Williams”.

I know these are folk tunes, but it’s as blatant as can be that the ideas in my arrangement are from Gustav and Ralph. While I tweaked and pared down the variations - the whole set was inspired by the idea of using variations in the middle section.

I would like to add a footnote on my part that acknowledges The Session as the source and “Falkbeer” for writing the abc file that served as the basis for the middle section. That username has no activity in over a decade - does anyone who is still around know anything about her/him?

Re: Greensleeves

It’s definitely not Irish, nor was it written by Henry V111. The first mention of it is in Registers of the Stationers Company in London in September 1580. Late in the reign of Elizabeth 1. It is referred to as “A new Northern Dittye of the Lady Green Sleeves.” The oldest notation and oldest version is not he one that everyone knows, but rather one in a lute MS in Cambridge, England. Greensleeves to a Ground is very much the same and the A and B parts are likely the oldest versions that we have. The rest of the parts (or divisions) are improvisations on those A and B parts. This predates that version that most people know, which comes form the William Ballet lute MS from (I think) 1597. Greensleeves is a very elastic and adaptable tune which, being modal, exists in a wide variety of guises, some of which are not even recognizable to most people.
